title: The dragon king's daughter (Kern ch. 11)
hookLine: in this chapter the young naga princess offers a jewel and awakens in an instant, to the disciples' surprise

lines: A GIRL FROM UNDER THE SEA.
cards: Someone in the middle of chapter eleven says, out loud, that he doesn't believe it. Not a scoffer in the back row: a bodhisattva named Prajnakuta, attendant to the Buddha of the jeweled tower.

He's just been told that a young girl, daughter of the dragon king who rules under the sea, has reached the very edge of awakening. He knows the road is supposed to take ages, lifetimes, countless gifts and sacrifices.
A child, from the ocean, from a family of serpents? No. Then she walks in.

teach.h: MANJUSHRI COMES UP FROM THE SEA.
teach.b: First, the setup. The bodhisattva Manjushri rises out of the ocean, where he's been teaching the Lotus in the palace of Sagara, the naga king. Nagas are serpent beings of the waters; English often calls them dragons.
Has anyone there taken this teaching in deeply enough to awaken quickly? Prajnakuta asks. Yes, says Manjushri: Sagara's young daughter, wise, kind, steady in meditation.
The Buddha himself strove for ages, Prajnakuta says; he can't believe a girl could do it in a moment. Then the girl appears, bows, and praises the Buddha.
And the senior disciple Sariputra adds his own objection: a woman's body, he says, cannot reach buddhahood. Third, the jewel.
She offers the Buddha a jewel of enormous worth, and he accepts it at once. She turns to the two doubters: was that quick? Very quick, they say.
Watch me, she says, awaken faster than that. Fourth, the instant.

Before the whole assembly, the text shows her form changing to a male one, and she appears in a world to the south, seated under a bodhi tree, fully awake, teaching. Prajnakuta and Sariputra go silent.
That change of body is read in more than one way. Some readers hear the old assumption that a woman must first become a man.
Others point out that she awakens anyway, faster than the objection can finish, and hear the objection answered.
The chapter ends with two senior figures silent, and a young girl teaching.

how: In Mahayana communities that read the Lotus Sutra, the naga king's daughter is remembered as the girl who awakened in an instant, and traditions read the change of her body in different ways.

games.q: what does “the dragon king's daughter” mean?
o: a sea goddess who guards the Lotus Sutra's scrolls
a young naga girl who awakens while senior figures doubt her
a princess who gives up her jewels to become a nun

games.q: in an instant: tap the pairs.
p: rises from the sea, where he taught the Lotus
objects: a woman's body can't be a Buddha

s: the senior disciples welcome her right away
Prajnakuta says he can't believe it, and Sariputra objects. both go silent at the end.
the Buddha accepts her jewel at once
she asks the doubters if that was quick, then says watch me awaken faster.
traditions all read her change of body the same way
some hear an old limit on women; others hear the objection answered as she awakens anyway.

games.q: you're the naga king's daughter. two senior figures have just said, in front of everyone, that you can't do this. what do you do?
o: argue with them until they agree.
offer your jewel, then awaken in front of them.
games.why: she offers a jewel, the Buddha accepts it at once, and she awakens faster than that. the doubters go silent.

practice: Bring to mind one young person you know, a niece, a student, a new hire, and something they said or did that you brushed off.
For a few breaths, hold the real possibility that they saw something you didn't, and let the doubt go quiet, the way Prajnakuta's did.

wordCard.voice: The dragon king's daughter. A young naga girl, doubted by two senior figures, offers a jewel and awakens in front of everyone. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: a serpent being of the waters, often called a dragon in English; the dragon king's people.

carryVoice: Your line: in an instant. Faster than the objection could finish. Same time tomorrow.

sources.ref: Saddharma-pundarika, ch. 11 (Kern's numbering; ch. 12 in Kumarajiva's Chinese)
